absent: Grace-period sequence management, quiescent-state tracking, and tree traversal beyond the stall-check predicates.
Tree node and root lock implementations, interrupt handling, and memory-ordering guarantees.
Full flavor operation table including callback, barrier, polling, stall, lag, and synchronization operations.
Forward-progress flood and non-blocking test internals and callback list processing.
Torture framework primitives for thread creation, shutdown detection, stutter, scheduling, affinity, and statistics.
No-callback mask ownership, CPU hotplug interaction, and migration semantics.
Debug-objects duplicate-detection behavior and allocation failure paths.
Timer, wait-queue, atomic, mutex, and allocation primitive implementations referenced as stubs.
Module parameters, boot completion detection, and overall test orchestration outside these fragments.

findings.text: Provides a helper that confines the calling context to the set of no-callback CPUs when that set is defined and nonempty, reporting affinity failures as warnings.
Provides an accessor that reports the configured priority used for grace-period kernel threads.

A grace-period start stall warning is possible only in a debug configuration while no grace period is active, requested sequence work remains outstanding, the grace-period thread handle is stable, recent request and activity timestamps are older than the configured delay, and no prior warning has been recorded.

Stall evaluation serializes on the supplied tree node lock with interrupts saved, additionally takes the root node lock without changing interrupt state when the two nodes differ, and holds coverage across the final warning flag update so concurrent observers converge on a single report; locks are released in reverse order on every exit.

Stall detection re-evaluates progress, sequence demand, activity freshness and the warned state once without locks, again under the leaf lock, and a final time under leaf plus root coverage, so transient progress or concurrent warnings suppress duplicate reports.

Each forward-progress slot carries its own synchronization, a callback list with head and tail linkage, and a numeric identity distinguishing the coordinating slot from follower slots; the set of slots and their thread handles are published through globals.

Forward-progress testing runs one coordinator and zero or more followers driven by a shared sequence counter; the coordinator pauses, clears emergency stop, reports drained callback maxima, and advances the sequence, while followers sleep until the sequence moves or shutdown is requested, after which each iteration exercises configured callback and stall-sensitive paths and honors stutter control.

Forward-progress setup bounds the requested thread count by the CPU count, disables itself when the selected operations lack required synchronization, callback flooding, stall duration or barrier support or conflict with CPU stall and preemption tests, normalizes timing divisors, allocates and initializes per-slot state, publishes it under a mutex, registers low-memory notification, and creates one thread per slot with partial-count rollback on failure; teardown stops threads, unregisters notification, clears the published pointer under the same mutex, and frees allocations.

Barrier testing uses per-worker wait queues and thread handles plus shared invoked and outstanding counters and a phase indicator; the coordinator and workers rendezvous through counter depletion and a central wait queue.

Barrier episodes reset counters, publish a new phase with ordering guarantees, wake all workers, wait for all callbacks to be queued, invoke the flavor barrier operation, and account success versus invocation-count mismatch with an extended recovery wait that re-invokes the barrier until counts converge or shutdown arrives.

Barrier testing is skipped when no callbacks are configured or when the flavor lacks callback or barrier operations; otherwise it initializes counters, allocates worker state, initializes each worker wait queue, starts one worker per callback slot, and starts the coordinator, propagating thread-creation failures.

Forward-progress publication and teardown are serialized by a dedicated mutex, each forward-progress slot has an initialized spin synchronization object, and ten statically defined mutexes exist as a pool for torture locking exercises.
Read-exit coordination uses separate stop-request and stopped-acknowledgment flags plus a dedicated wait queue to hand shutdown from cleanup to the test thread.

Read-exit testing repeatedly spawns a short-lived child that idles until asked to stop and then performs a single read, reaps each child promptly while counting episodes, synchronizes for reclamation between bursts, observes an inter-burst delay that is interruptible by shutdown, and on exit publishes completion with ordering before waking cleanup and then idles until the framework stops it.

Boost testing is enabled only for explicit boost modes with flavor boost support and grace-period polling operations available and a nonzero grace-period thread priority; an excessively low priority produces a one-time advisory and disables the test.

Torture worker threads share a common lifecycle of optional boot and affinity setup, a loop that exits on framework shutdown request, periodic stutter checks with scheduling priority normalization, and a stopping announcement on return.

Preemption testing waits between episodes with small timing variation, cycles through online processors, attempts migration to each target with retry on failure, briefly elevates scheduling class while restoring wide affinity and delaying, then returns to normal scheduling and honors stutter control.

Grace-period wraparound lag testing alternates between an enabled interval with a configured lag magnitude and a disabled interval with zero lag, deriving the two dwell times from cycle and active minute parameters, rearming for the opposite phase until shutdown is requested; initialization validates positive timing and arms the first disabled dwell, while cleanup cancels timing and forces zero lag.

Module teardown handles concurrent cleanup races and missing operation tables, optionally exercises nonmaskable-interrupt paths and debug output, stops workers in a fixed order covering preemption, read-exit, barrier, forward-progress, stall, writer, no-callback toggles, hotplug, readers and fake writers with deallocation of their handle arrays, samples grace-period state, stops statistics and forcing threads, removes boost hotplug state when applicable, performs a final barrier and flavor-specific cleanup, dumps memory, statistics and error segments, and reports failure, hotplug-affected or success outcomes before closing cleanup and unregistering slow-path and lag hooks.

Duplicate-callback checking is performed only when debug-object support is compiled in and required flavor operations exist; it holds a read section open to pin a grace period, queues the same stack and heap objects repeatedly with distinct leak and error callbacks, then barriers, logs start and completion advisories, and destroys and frees the objects, where the leak callback intentionally does nothing and invocation of the duplicate error callback indicates an unexpected second grace period and is logged.

Nonmaskable-interrupt style testing either walks processors and requests a task dump of a neighboring processor under disabled preemption with long pauses when built into the kernel, or emits a one-time warning when a nonzero count is requested from modular builds.
A periodic synchronization helper invokes the flavor synchronous grace-period operation approximately once per few thousand calls when such an operation exists.
Out-of-memory handling for forward-progress testing is wired through a statically initialized notifier registration that directs events to the torture low-memory handler.
Boost hotplug lifecycle retains a persistent state identifier so that initialization and teardown can conditionally add and remove the same hotplug observer.
